title: Full vs Partial Renovation: How to Choose for Your Winnipeg Home
metaTitle: Full vs Partial Renovation in Winnipeg: How to Decide
metaDescription: Full renovation or room-by-room upgrades? A decision table, what older Winnipeg homes hide behind the walls, and how to phase work without paying twice.
excerpt: A full renovation fixes everything at once; partial upgrades spread the work and the cost over time. The right choice depends on the condition of your house, your plans and how much disruption you can live with. Here is a practical way to decide.
answer: Choose a full renovation when the wiring, plumbing, insulation or layout need work in several rooms, or when you want the whole house finished to one standard at once. Choose partial upgrades when those systems are sound and only one or two rooms hold you back. Many homes suit a phased plan that does the system work first.

faqs.q: When does a partial renovation make more sense than a full one?
faqs.a: When the house's wiring, plumbing, insulation and layout are in reasonable shape and only one or two rooms hold you back. A partial upgrade then gives most of the benefit with less cost and disruption. It also suits budgets that work year by year, as long as each stage fits a plan for the whole house.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to renovate everything at once?
faqs.a: Per room, it often is, because set-up, demolition, permits and trade visits happen once instead of several times. It costs more up front, though, and means more disruption at one time. If the budget is the limit, a phased plan that does the system work first keeps many of the same savings.

faqs.q: Can we live in the house during a full renovation?
faqs.a: Often, yes, if the work is staged in sections and a kitchen and bathroom stay usable. Sometimes it is faster to move out for a few weeks. Both options can be laid out at the on-site visit, so you can weigh the time saved against the disruption before you decide.

faqs.q: What if problems turn up once the walls are open?
faqs.a: Older homes in particular can reveal water damage, old wiring or altered framing once walls come down. The work should stop, you should be shown what was found, and the fix should be priced before work continues. A contingency in your budget means a discovery changes the plan, not the whole project.

faqs.q: How do I know if my house needs a full renovation?
faqs.a: Look at the systems and the layout, not just the finishes. Signs include wiring that cannot handle modern loads, plumbing problems in several places, cold rooms from poor insulation, or a layout that no longer suits how you live. An on-site visit can separate what needs doing now from what can wait.

blocks.x: Most renovation plans start with a list: the kitchen is tired, the bathroom leaks, the basement is unfinished, the windows are drafty. The big decision is whether to tackle the list all at once or one room at a time. Both can be the right answer. The difference is usually in the parts of the house you cannot see.
What is the difference between a full and a partial renovation?

A full renovation brings most of the house to a common standard at once: the layout, systems such as wiring and plumbing, and the finishes. A partial renovation, or room-by-room upgrade, renovates one area at a time, such as the kitchen or a bathroom, while the rest of the house stays as it is.

Between the two sits the phased renovation: one plan for the whole house, built in stages over months or years. It is often the most realistic option for a family that needs to live in the house and pay for the work as it goes.
How do you decide between them?

Start with the condition of the house, not the finishes. If the wiring, plumbing, insulation or layout need work across the house, a full renovation usually avoids opening the same walls twice. If those are sound and one room is the problem, a partial upgrade gives most of the benefit with less cost and disruption.

blocks.x: What do older Winnipeg homes hide behind the walls?

Older houses can hide lead paint, materials that may contain asbestos, outdated wiring, and framing changed by earlier renovations. Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably contains lead-based paint, and that vermiculite insulation may contain asbestos. Finding these early can tip a partial job toward a fuller one, or at least change the order of work.

That does not mean every older house needs to be gutted. It means testing and an honest look at the systems should come before design. Health Canada advises having a professional test for asbestos before renovating, and testing old paint before sanding or stripping it. Our guide to [renovating a character home in Winnipeg](/blog/renovating-a-character-home-in-winnipeg) covers what to check first.
Can you phase a renovation without paying twice?

Yes, if the phases follow the house's systems rather than its rooms. Plan the whole house first, then do the work that runs behind walls, such as the electrical service, main plumbing lines and insulation, before the finishes it would disturb. Each phase should leave the house usable and avoid tearing out recent work later.
Make a whole-house plan, even if you build it in stages.
Do structural and system work first: foundation repairs, the electrical service, main plumbing lines and insulation.
Renovate rooms that share walls or plumbing together, such as a kitchen and a bathroom stacked above it.
Leave purely cosmetic work, such as paint, light fixtures and hardware, for later.
Get each phase permitted and inspected where required, so the next phase builds on approved work.

On permits: the City of Winnipeg lists basement development, additions and many home renovations, including kitchens, bathrooms and open-concept changes, among projects that may need a building permit, while cosmetic work such as painting and flooring does not. We coordinate permits and inspections with the City or your local municipality.
How do cost and timeline compare?

A full renovation costs more at once but usually avoids repeating the set-up, demolition and trade visits that come with doing rooms separately. Partial upgrades spread the cost over time. On timing, most of our whole home renovations take 8 to 16 weeks, while a single kitchen or bathroom takes much less.

What should you ask at the on-site visit?

Ask questions that separate what needs doing now from what can wait. A good visit should leave you knowing which systems are near the end of their life, which rooms are linked by plumbing or structure, what needs a permit, and whether the work can be staged so you can stay in the house.
Which systems in my house need work now, and which can wait?
If I renovate this room now, what would a later phase have to reopen?
Which parts of the plan need permits?
Can the work be staged so we can live here?
What should be tested before demolition?
